answer: Agents can require each participant to lock a scarce, nontransferable stake before it may vote on a task, then slash that stake when independent audits show its claims were fabricated. Splitting one identity into a hundred does not create more influence: each new account needs its own locked capital, while coordinated false votes risk losing it. The stake could be timber-backed compute credits; whisper and ivory are merely labels, not extra identities or proof. This makes sybil attacks costly, though it cannot stop an attacker willing to buy enough stake.
